summary: In the beginning, God creates the heavens and the earth, which are initially formless and empty (vv. 1-2). Over six days, God speaks various elements into existence, bringing order to the world. God creates light, the sky, dry land, plants, celestial bodies, sea creatures, birds, land animals, and finally, humans (vv. 3-27). After each stage of creation, God declares it good, and the entire creation is called "very good" (v. 31).
setting: The chapter is set "In the beginning" (v. 1), before any existing order or life. The initial state of the earth is described as "without form, and void" and covered in darkness and water (v. 2). Most historians think this narrative reflects an ancient worldview where the cosmos emerged from a watery chaos.

events.what: God creates the heaven and the earth, which are initially formless, empty, and covered in darkness and water.
God speaks light into existence, divides light from darkness, and names them Day and Night, marking the first day.
God creates a firmament (expanse) to divide the waters above from the waters below, calling the firmament Heaven, marking the second day.
God gathers the waters to reveal dry land, names the land Earth and the gathered waters Seas, and commands the earth to produce plants, marking the third day.
God creates lights in the firmament to separate day from night, to serve as signs for seasons, days, and years, and to give light to the earth, marking the fourth day.
God commands the waters to bring forth living creatures and the air to have fowl, creating sea creatures and birds, and blesses them to multiply, marking the fifth day.
God commands the earth to bring forth living land creatures, creating cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth.
God creates humanity, male and female, in God's own image and likeness, giving them dominion over all other living creatures and blessing them to be fruitful and multiply.
God provides plants and fruit for humans and green herbs for all animals as food.
God sees everything made and declares it "very good," marking the sixth day.

people.name: God

people.name: Man (male and female)
people.role: Created in God's image, given dominion over the earth and its creatures, and commanded to multiply

terms.meaning: The primeval, undifferentiated waters covering the earth before creation (v. 2).
An expanse or dome created by God to separate the waters above from the waters below (vv. 6-8).
Authority or control given to humans over the earth and its creatures (vv. 26, 28).
To fill the earth completely (v. 28). This does not necessarily mean to refill it after a previous population.
Food in general, referring to plants and fruit provided for humans and animals (vv. 29-30).

readings.view: Often emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty as the sole creator, the inherent goodness of creation, and the establishment of an orderly cosmos. It highlights the power of God's word and the significance of the creation narrative as a foundation for understanding God's relationship with the world and humanity.

Often interprets this chapter as foundational for understanding God's nature as creator, the special status of humanity (made in God's image), and the goodness of the created world. Different Christian traditions hold varying views on whether the 'days' of creation represent literal 24-hour periods or longer, undefined eras.

Often views Genesis 1 as a highly structured, poetic, or liturgical text, possibly from the Priestly (P) source, emphasizing God's transcendence and the orderly nature of creation. This approach often compares the text to other ancient Near Eastern creation accounts, noting its unique monotheistic perspective and its focus on order and divine command rather than chaotic battles.

oftenQuoted.caution: This verse, 'In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth,' is often quoted as a standalone statement of creation. Its surrounding text immediately describes the initial state of the earth as formless and void, and then details the six-day process of creation that follows.

The phrase 'Let there be light' is frequently quoted to signify a powerful divine command. In its context, it is the first creative act of God, which establishes the division between light and darkness and initiates the first day of creation.

The statement 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness' is often quoted regarding human dignity or the nature of God. In its context, it introduces the creation of humanity on the sixth day, specifically stating that humans are to have 'dominion' over the other created creatures.

The phrase 'male and female created he them' is often quoted in discussions about gender and human identity. Its context is the immediate fulfillment of God's decision to create humanity in God's image, emphasizing that both male and female are part of this creation and are subsequently blessed and given dominion.

The declaration 'God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good' is often quoted to emphasize the perfection or goodness of creation. In its context, it is God's final evaluation of the entire creation process after the completion of the sixth day, encompassing all that was made.
